## PART 3: MAIN PROJECT (Moran's I) {.unnumbered}

**CREATE A NEW HEADING CALLED CHICAGO PROJECT**

You are an urban planner working for the City of Chicago, tasked with helping decide where to prioritise future investment in urban development, green spaces and tree planting.

Your office is concerned about geographical inequalities across the city. In particular, you want to understand whether differences in wealth, poverty and housing conditions are becoming more geographically concentrated or dispersed over time, and whether similar patterns exist in the distribution of urban tree cover.

You have been given census tract data for **2010 and 2018**. Your task is to use spatial statistics, including **Global Moran's I and LISA**, to investigate how these patterns have changed, identify neighbourhoods where inequalities persist, and consider what your findings might mean for future planning decisions.

<br><br>

### STEP 6: Explore the data {.unnumbered}

#### Dataset: Chicago Census Tracts (2018)

- **The `ChicagoTracts_2018` dataset contains demographic, socioeconomic and environmental information for census tracts across Chicago for the year 2018.**

- **The `ChicagoTracts_2010` dataset contains demographic, socioeconomic and environmental information for census tracts across Chicago for the year 2010.**

- In both, each row represents a census tract, with an associated polygon showing its geographical boundaries.

The dataset contains the following variables:

| Variable | Description |
|----|----|
| `GEOID` | Unique census tract identifier |
| `arealand_sqmiles` | Land area of the tract (square miles) |
| `canopy_2018` | Percentage of the tract covered by tree canopy |
| `population_2018` | Total population |
| `pop_density_2018` | Population per square mile |
| `pct_poverty_2018` | Percentage of residents living below the poverty threshold |
| `med_income_2018` | Median household income (\$) |
| `med_rent_2018` | Median monthly rent (\$) |
| `med_value_2018` | Median home value (\$) |
| `pct_vacant_2018` | Percentage of housing units that are vacant |
| `pct_white_2018` | Percentage of residents identified as White |
| `pct_black_2018` | Percentage of residents identified as Black |
| `pct_hispanic_2018` | Percentage of residents identified as Hispanic or Latino |
| `pct_degree_2018` | Percentage of residents with a college degree |
| `geometry` | Census tract boundaries (MULTIPOLYGON) |

Most variables come from the **2018 American Community Survey (ACS)**, which provides census tract-level estimates of population characteristics, income, poverty, housing and education. Tree canopy coverage was calculated separately using **LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging)** data.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# You need to have run your library code chunk with the tmap library in it.

treemap_2010 <- tm_shape(ChicagoTracts_2010) +
   tm_polygons(fill = "canopy_2010",

# You need to change ChicagoTracts_2018 to whatever you called the files.

   tm_polygons(fill = "canopy_2018",
               fill.scale  = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", values = "brewer.greens"),
               fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Tree cover 2018 (%)"),
               col = NA)

# This will plot the maps together rather than one at a time
tmap_arrange(treemap_2010,treemap_2018)
```

### STEP 7: Calculate the change in your variables {.unnumbered}

We now want to calculate the difference between 2010 and 2018, as that might help with visualising any changes. This is more complex than it might first appear!

- **Always start with the later time-stamp** (e.g. 2018 - 2010). You want increases to be positive and decreases negative

<br>

- **Use 'percentage points' when comparing percentages** (e.g. percentage tree cover, percent of people in poverty). This becomes an issue when we try to calculate differences, because it's easy to end up with a percentage of a percentage and a lot of confusion (see the cartoon below!). Instead, we tend to use "percentage points".
  - A percentage point the simple arithmetic difference between two percentage values. \
    Value1(%) - Value2(%). E.g. if your index of 20% decreases by a percentage point, it means it goes from 20% to 19%.
  - If you calculated the percentage change (19-20)/20 you would have to say your value fell by 5%. What you *mean* is 5% of the previous percentage of 20% (so 1% overall), but people will have already tuned out.
  

```{r, P2-XKCD, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="For a more detailed explanation, see https://www.explainxkcd.com/wiki/index.php/985:_Percentage_Points", out.width="60%"}
knitr::include_graphics('./index_images/im_P2_XKCD985.png')
```

<br>

- **Use raw values, or percentage change when comparing numeric variables.** Some (like population) are numeric (e.g. the population in 2010 was 1249 and in 2018, the population was 1502). So in this case, we can either

  - Calculate at the raw change (1502 - 1249 = 253 more people), which is simple to understand, but over a whole map, areas where the population was high to start with might swamp any view of what's happening
  - OR.. we calculate the percentage change. (1502 - 1249)/1249 = 0.203. So the population went up in my made up example by 20%. This is not a percentage point!
  
<br>  

- **For monetary variables, such as income, rent or housing value, you must also take inflation into account** (temporal autocorrelation!). If not, all you'll see on the map is that life "became more expensive", which would likely swamp any spatial pattern.  A simple method to achieve this is to convert the 2010 values into 2018 dollars using an inflation adjustment factor, the ratio of a price index. 

   * A price index tracks the cost of a typical "basket" of goods and services over time. The most common one in the US is the Consumer Price Index (CPI), published by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
   * In the ACS 5-year estimates, every dollar value is already adjusted to the LAST year of the survey period. So the 2006-2010 data are in 2010 dollars, and the 2014-2018 data are in 2018 dollars.
   * To put 2010 dollars into 2018 dollars, we multiply the 2010 values by the ratio of the two index values:
   
   2010ValueIn2018Dollars = 2010Value/2018Value
 
$$
      \text{2010 value in "2018 dollars"} = \text{2010 value} \times \frac{\text{CPI}_{2018}}{\text{CPI}_{2010}}
      
$$
   * The Census Bureau recommends the "R-CPI-U-RS" index for this (the CPI for all urban consumers, research series), where $\text{CPI}_{2010}$ is the annual average for 2010 and $\text{CPI}_{2018}$ is the annual average for 2018. You can find those numbers here https://www.bls.gov/cpi/research-series/r-cpi-u-rs-allitems.pdf (or by googling the R-CPI-U-RS annual average for a specific year)
   
Given all that, here's the summary for our dataset

| Variable type | Our variables | Change to calculate |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Percentages | canopy, pct_poverty, pct_vacant, pct_white, pct_black, pct_hispanic, pct_degree | 2018 - 2010, in percentage points |
| Counts | population (pop_density gives the same percentage change, as the tract area is fixed) | raw change, or percentage change |
| Money | med_income, med_rent, med_value | adjust 2010 to 2018 dollars, then percentage change |


<br>

- **[7A]** Copy the code below into your report, but BEFORE YOU RUN IT, find the correct values for cpi_2010 and cpi_2018 from the resources you just read about, and add them in the appropriate spot. <br><br>
E.g. replace ANS at the top of the code chunk with the actual numbers from your reading
<br><br>
You might also need to replace ChicagoTracts_2010 and ChicagoTracts_2018 with whatever you called them.



```{r, eval=FALSE}


# Get the Consumer price index in 2010 and 2018
# THIS WILL BREAK UNTIL YOU REPLACE ANS WITH ACTUAL NUMBERS.
cpi_2010 <- ANS
cpi_2018 <- ANS 

inflation_adjustment <- cpi_2010/cpi_2018


ChicagoTracts_Change <- ChicagoTracts_2018 |>
   left_join(st_drop_geometry(ChicagoTracts_2010) |> select(-arealand_sqmiles),
             by = "GEOID") |>
   mutate(
      #--- Percentages: 2018 minus 2010, in percentage points
      # canopy is a percentage, its just not in the variable name
      chg_canopy      = canopy_2018       - canopy_2010,
      chg_poverty     = pct_poverty_2018  - pct_poverty_2010,
      chg_vacant      = pct_vacant_2018   - pct_vacant_2010,
      chg_white       = pct_white_2018    - pct_white_2010,
      chg_black       = pct_black_2018    - pct_black_2010,
      chg_hispanic    = pct_hispanic_2018 - pct_hispanic_2010,
      chg_degree      = pct_degree_2018   - pct_degree_2010,
      
      #--- Counts: percent change
      chg_population  = 100 * (population_2018 - population_2010) / population_2010,
      
      #--- Dollars: percent change after adjusting for inflation
      chg_income      = 100 * (med_income_2018 / (med_income_2010 * inflation_adjustment) - 1),
      chg_rent        = 100 * (med_rent_2018   / (med_rent_2010   * inflation_adjustment) - 1),
      chg_value       = 100 * (med_value_2018  / (med_value_2010  * inflation_adjustment) - 1)
   ) |>
   #--- Keep just the ID, land area and the change columns
   select(GEOID, arealand_sqmiles, starts_with("chg_")) 
   
   



```



<br>
